## The likelihood

![](images/likelihood_data_model_dist.svg){.step}

::: {.fragment}
Each observation gets a distribution around the model output,
$p(\text{data point } i \mid \theta)$. If they are conditionally independent given $\theta$:

$$\log p(\text{data} \mid \theta) = \sum_{i} \log p(\text{data point } i \mid \theta)$$
:::

##  {.center}

![](images/big_picture_functions_base.svg){.tall}

$$p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$$

## Why sample?

![](images/rs_n_00100000.png){.step}

$p(\theta \mid \text{data})$ is the probability distribution of a random
variable, so we can sample from it.

## Rejection sampling

![](images/RS23.png){.step}

It draws from the posterior, but the acceptance rate collapses as the number of
parameters grows.

## Metropolis-Hastings

![](images/MH6.png){.step}

Propose $\theta^*$ from where you are, and accept with probability

$$r = \min\left(1, \frac{f(\theta^*)\,q(\theta \mid \theta^*)}{f(\theta)\,q(\theta^* \mid \theta)}\right)$$

## NUTS

Random-walk proposals ignore the shape of the posterior. Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo uses the **gradient** to move with it, and [NUTS]{.alert} adapts the step
size and stops each trajectory when it turns back on itself.

::: {.fragment}
Usually no proposal tuning at all, and therefore a sensible default if it can
be used.
:::
